# Use AI to Widen the Search, Not to Choose the Question

## Narration

[Visual: A researcher’s question at the center of a blank canvas. Candidate papers, concepts, and methods gradually appear around it as labeled cards.]

When an AI system proposes twenty dissertation topics in thirty seconds, it can feel as if topic selection has become easy. But generating possible directions is not the same as identifying a research question that is original, consequential, and defensible.

The useful role for AI is narrower: widen and organize the search. The researcher must still choose the question.

[Visual: Two-stage diagram: “Explore broadly” followed by “Investigate promising paths.” A revisable evidence graph grows beside it.]

A commentary in *Nature Machine Intelligence*, discussing the DeepEvidence system, reports that informed, staged exploration can outperform undirected searching across large, heterogeneous knowledge bases. The system first searches broadly, then follows promising mechanistic and citation links in depth. It records entities, relationships, observations, and provenance in an evolving evidence graph. [claim:01-c1]

That does not prove the same workflow will produce more original dissertations. The article is commentary on another system, and its evidence concerns structured exploration—not the long-term quality of researcher-selected topics. Still, it suggests a practical workflow: ask AI to construct a revisable map rather than deliver a verdict.

[Visual: A table with four columns: candidate question, supporting evidence, contradictory evidence, unresolved dependency.]

For each candidate direction, have the system identify relevant literatures, competing findings, assumptions, and missing evidence. Then inspect the primary sources yourself. Provenance can show where an assertion came from; it cannot establish that an apparent gap is important, scientifically tractable, or truly novel.

MIT professor Sasha Rakhlin assigns that evaluative responsibility to the graduate researcher. In his account, students should learn to formulate problems, audit model outputs, reproduce results, and defend their choices. He also distinguishes obtaining a solution from understanding why it works, what generalizes, and what should be asked next. [claim:01-c2]

[Visual: The AI-generated map stops at a gate labeled “Researcher judgment.” Beyond it are three questions: Novel? Significant? Dependency-safe?]

Practitioner testimony points in the same direction. On the *Latent Space* podcast, AI researcher Alex Zhang says that an expert who understands a problem can sometimes guide a model more efficiently than a brute-force search consuming hundreds of billions or even a trillion tokens. He qualifies the observation: the overall trend is not yet clear. [claim:01-c3]

Expertise, on this view, is not merely another input to automate. It determines which branch deserves attention and which attractive-looking premise should be abandoned.

The cost of skipping that judgment can propagate. Retraction Watch reported that, in a large release of AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, roughly half of the results were released unconfirmed. A later sign error invalidated one argument and constructions used by two dependent papers. This episode does not show that AI-assisted topic discovery is generally unreliable. It shows why scale and speed cannot substitute for validation.

[Visual: One faulty premise card connects to several dependent cards; the links turn red.]

Taken together, these sources support a division of labor: use AI to generate candidates, trace connections, expose dependencies, and keep the search revisable. Reserve gap validation and final topic choice for researchers who can test novelty, significance, and the strength of the underlying evidence. [claim:01-c4]

Structured exploration may still reveal genuinely unexpected connections, and future systems may become better judges of novelty. Current evidence, however, does not tell us whether AI-selected questions yield more original dissertations over time.

So the practical rule is simple: let AI enlarge the map. Do not let it decide which destination deserves years of research.

## Production notes

- Target duration: approximately 4 minutes.
- Keep all evidence maps illustrative; do not depict fabricated paper counts, novelty scores, or performance statistics.
- Display source type on first mention: “scholarly commentary,” “faculty perspective,” “practitioner testimony,” or “reported case.”
- Put each claim marker on screen when its corresponding sentence is narrated.
- Use the dependency animation only as a conceptual illustration of cascading error, not as a reconstruction of the manuscripts.

# Verification Architecture Matters More Than Fluent Reasoning

## Narration

[Visual: A polished AI explanation appears on screen. A stamp reading “Plausible” appears, followed by a separate unchecked box labeled “Verified.”]

A fluent explanation can make an answer easier to trust. It cannot make the answer true.

For AI-assisted research and writing, the important question is not, “Does the model sound as though it reasoned carefully?” It is, “What independent checks can make its claims fail visibly?”

[Visual: A verification loop: define the problem, generate candidates, execute checks, inspect sources and dependencies, repair, repeat.]

Evidence from combinatorial optimization illustrates the difference between direct prompting and a constrained workflow. A *Nature Machine Intelligence* paper evaluated a framework called LACE across 36 benchmark problems. Its average score was 0.945, compared with 0.870 for the strongest existing LLM-based method and 0.571 for direct prompting using the same model backbone. [claim:02-c1]

The authors locate the gain in the framework rather than the model alone. LACE supplies a verified problem contract, input and output schemas, a tool library, a portfolio of specialist heuristics, feasibility checks, and iterative selection and repair.

[Visual: Bar chart labeled exactly: LACE 0.945; strongest existing LLM-based method 0.870; direct prompting 0.571. Caption: “36 CO-Bench problems.”]

This is strong evidence for that bounded optimization setting—not a universal estimate of performance in scholarly writing. Formal feasibility is easier to test in code and mathematics than evidence quality or interpretation in qualitative and empirical research. The study also examined only four author-formulated new problems beyond the benchmark.

But its design principle transfers: establish the contract before asking for prose. Specify the question, admissible evidence, definitions, assumptions, output format, and conditions that would invalidate the answer.

Why not simply inspect the model’s reasoning text? A *Nature Machine Intelligence* Perspective argues that reasoning tokens can contribute to producing an answer and can sometimes read like logical steps, while still not faithfully explaining the process that generated the result. The authors call attention to a trust-calibration problem: plausibility can increase confidence without justifying it. [claim:02-c3]

[Visual: The model’s rationale enters a box labeled “Candidate explanation,” not “Evidence.”]

Treat a rationale as material to test, not as an audit trail. Recalculate quantities. Run code and feasibility checks. Open every cited source. Confirm that the source supports the precise sentence. Trace which conclusions depend on which assumptions.

A reported case shows why dependency checks matter. Retraction Watch described a sign error that invalidated an argument in one OpenAI manuscript and the construction used by two dependent manuscripts. Fourteen other manuscripts were revised with proof repairs, corrected statements, clearer hypotheses and dependencies, and one correction to an obsolete citation. [claim:02-c2]

The lesson is not that every use of AI produces this failure. It is that one unchecked premise can survive polished exposition and then propagate through dependent outputs.

[Visual: A claim-and-dependency ledger. One failed check highlights every downstream claim that requires reinspection.]

In a commercial SciSpace webinar, a reviewer summarizes the objective as using AI to make good research, not lots of research. [claim:02-c4] That is useful practitioner guidance, but it is not independent evidence that SciSpace’s products deliver the safeguards being recommended.

A related practitioner discussion about AlphaFold stresses the need to understand a model’s behavioral strengths and limitations before relying on it. This reinforces a practical standard: evaluate a tool within the task and conditions where you will actually use it.

Across these sources, the defensible inference is that AI assistance should be judged by its verification loop: explicit contracts, executable tools where available, external evidence, citation and dependency checks, and iterative repair. Fluency—and even apparent transparency—is not enough. [claim:02-c5]

The safest workflow therefore ends neither with the first answer nor with the first readable rationale. It ends when the important claims have survived checks that do not depend on the model merely sounding convincing.

## Production notes

- Target duration: approximately 4 minutes.
- The only quantitative chart should show the three reported LACE averages and the 36-problem benchmark context.
- Label the LACE result as domain-specific; do not visually imply a measured effect on general academic writing.
- Treat reasoning text as a candidate explanation in all graphics, never as a faithful internal trace.
- Put each claim marker on screen with the relevant narration.

# Authorship After Automation Means Auditable Responsibility

## Narration

[Visual: A polished manuscript fades into the background. In front of it appears a chain: contribution, evidence, verification, disclosure, correction.]

When AI contributes to literature review, analysis, or prose, authorship cannot be reduced to the question, “Who typed each sentence?” A more demanding question is: can the named author reconstruct, verify, and defend the work?

That is the core of auditable responsibility.

MIT professor Sasha Rakhlin argues that, in a growing number of fields, a polished paper is becoming a weaker signal of individual expertise. He proposes that evaluation should establish what a researcher contributed and accepts intellectual responsibility for, including when AI performed substantial parts of the work. [claim:03-c1]

[Visual: Contribution statement with fields for question formulation, data, analysis, verification, writing assistance, and final approval.]

For a researcher, that means being able to identify which ideas and decisions were yours; which tasks were delegated; which outputs were accepted, changed, or rejected; and why. It also means retaining enough evidence to reproduce central results and explain methodological choices.

Process records can help. Rakhlin suggests that tracing research workflows could preserve the lineage of ideas and make contributions—including those of graduate students—easier to recognize. But a record is not proof of understanding, and provenance is not correctness.

A *Nature Machine Intelligence* commentary makes that distinction explicit: recording where information originated does not necessarily make a conclusion valid. The literature itself may contain bias, conflicting results, uneven methods, or context-dependent effects. [claim:03-c2]

[Visual: A source card receives a “Provenance recorded” checkmark while “Claim validated” remains unchecked.]

So an auditable workflow needs more than prompt logs. For each important claim, preserve the cited source, the exact supporting passage or result, any relevant transformation or computation, and the dependencies connecting it to the conclusion. Then verify that chain independently.

A reviewer speaking in a commercial SciSpace webinar describes acceptable assistance in terms of continuity of intellectual ownership: it remains the researcher’s work, idea, and collected data. [claim:03-c3] That is a practitioner perspective presented by a company selling research tools, not independent validation of those products. Still, it identifies an important boundary: editing assistance does not transfer responsibility away from the researcher.

[Visual: The researcher remains at the center while tools assist with outlining, language revision, and evidence organization.]

Periodic Labs’ founders offer a more expansive view of process lineage. On the *Latent Space* podcast, they describe capturing conversations, intuitions, laboratory actions, computations, and code so that models can learn from the process of science rather than only its final outputs. [claim:03-c4]

That description is commercially interested founder testimony. It also exposes a tradeoff. Detailed lineage may support accountability and training, but it can burden researchers, reveal confidential ideas or data, and create surveillance-like records. The SciSpace webinar separately advises researchers to think carefully about data and privacy before sharing material with any AI system.

[Visual: A record-retention control with three labels: necessary, sensitive, unnecessary. No real laboratory data shown.]

The goal, then, is not to save everything. It is to keep proportionate records that allow consequential claims and contributions to be audited without exposing material that should remain private.

Correction is part of authorship too. Retraction Watch reported a case in which an error in one AI-generated mathematics manuscript affected two dependent papers. OpenAI’s stated response was to correct errors promptly and withdraw papers when no fix could be found. Responsibility therefore extends beyond initial release to dependent outputs, revisions, and withdrawal decisions.

Across the sources, responsible authorship is best understood as an auditable chain of contribution, evidence, verification, disclosure, and correction—not ownership of polished final prose alone. [claim:03-c5]

[Visual: Final checklist. “Can I explain my contribution? Trace the evidence? Reproduce the result? Verify the citations? Disclose material AI use? Correct the record?”]

No universal logging threshold will fit every discipline. Documentation can be excessive, and it cannot prove genuine understanding. But the human author should be able to answer those six questions—and accept responsibility when the chain fails.

## Production notes

- Target duration: approximately 4 minutes.
- Use generic document and workflow graphics; do not display simulated private prompts, unpublished data, or laboratory records.
- Visually distinguish provenance from validation throughout.
- Identify SciSpace and Periodic Labs statements as commercially interested practitioner or founder testimony.
- Put each claim marker on screen during the corresponding passage.
- The closing checklist is a synthesis of the cited evidence, not a universal policy standard.
